### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Cleveland and Lukes overlay the digitized 1935–40 HOLC "redlining" maps on 2018–19 school-district boundaries and school locations in 144 metropolitan areas and run enrollment-weighted, CBSA-fixed-effects difference-in-means regressions of district revenue, school expenditure, school racial composition, and SEDA achievement on HOLC grade, with D as the reference. The cross-sectional core is credible and worth citing: within the same metro, schools sitting inside formerly D-graded polygons enroll far more Black (36% vs. 22% in A polygons) and far fewer White students (14% vs. 44%), and score 0.64 SD lower than schools in A polygons (Table 5), with a monotone A–B–C–D gradient that holds in every region; districts composed mostly of D-graded land raise roughly half the local revenue per pupil of A districts (\$5,240 vs. an A–D gap of \$5,937), with state and federal aid closing about three-quarters of that gap (Table 2). Those level gaps are large, precisely estimated, and unlikely to be overturned by the design's known weaknesses. The rest of the paper needs qualification. First, the design is a raw within-metro contrast with no controls; since HOLC grades encoded the race, class, and housing stock neighborhoods already had in the 1930s (the paper says so on p.20), the A–D gaps bundle pre-existing differences with anything the maps added, and the paper never asks whether grade predicts outcomes conditional on current neighborhood SES. The Methods section calls the approach "conservative" and "correlational" (pp.9–10) and the Discussion says "not causal" (p.21), but the abstract ("the consequences of redlining persist today"), the introduction, and the policy section ("redlining's impacts on property values") say otherwise; readers should follow the Methods, not the abstract. Second, the published article contains an exhibit error unusual for a peer-reviewed journal: Figure 3, captioned as district per-pupil revenue in 2018 dollars from 1989 to 2018, is not a revenue figure. Its y-axes run 0.20–0.85, three of its four panels are pixel-for-pixel the Percent Black, Percent White, and Simpson's Index panels of Figure 4, its "federal revenue" panel shows A districts highest (the reverse of Table 2), and its four decadal points cannot contain the "2009–2010 spike" the text describes. Every finance-trend claim in the paper, including the Discussion's "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018," therefore rests on a supplemental table that does not travel with the PDF. Third, the prose misreports the tables in several places a reader is likely to quote: a Northeast D-school score of "−0.023 SD" that is −0.225 in Table 5; Midwest school spending gaps called "statistically significant" that carry no stars; "virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends when all three national coefficients are significant at p<.01; state/local school spending gaps called "insignificant" in the Discussion that the Results and Table 3 show as significant; and a Table 1 performance sample of 5,124 schools against Table 5 Ns of 6,890, 5,193, and 6,183. Fourth, the paper's most interesting substantive result, that schools in D polygons spend the most per pupil even though D districts raise the least (Table 3 vs. Table 2), is under-sold, never reconciled with a school-level district-fixed-effects model, and omitted from the abstract, whose title word "Funding" invites the opposite reading. There is no data or code statement despite fully public inputs. The right posture is: cite the paper for the within-metro descriptive gaps in Tables 2, 4, and 5, quoting numbers from the tables rather than the text; do not cite it for finance trends over time, for causal effects of the HOLC maps, for property values as the mechanism, or for "underfunded" schools in redlined neighborhoods; and treat the 2021 EdWorkingPaper version (ai21-363) as the first public statement of these findings.

#### Key Strengths

- A new, reusable linkage at scale: HOLC polygons joined to 1,760 districts and roughly 9,000–9,700 schools across 144 CBSAs, entirely from public data (Mapping Inequality, TIGER/Line, NCES EDGE and CCD, F-33, NERD\$, SEDA 4.0), with an explicit area-weighting formula and discretization cutpoints (p.10). Others can extend it.
- The cross-sectional level gaps are large, precisely estimated, monotone across grades, and consistent across all four Census regions: an A–D average-score gap of 0.643 SD (SE 0.04; regional range 0.541–0.753) (Table 5), A–D gaps of −0.14 in share Black and +0.30 in share White (Table 4), and an A–D local-revenue gap of \$5,937 (SE \$1,228), significant in every region (Table 2).
- Tables 2–5 are complete and internally consistent: coefficients, CBSA-clustered SEs, R², F, and N for every model; regional Ns sum exactly to national Ns in every panel; and the federal, state, and local revenue coefficients in Table 2 sum to the total-revenue coefficients.
- The district-revenue versus school-expenditure contrast (Table 2 vs. Table 3) is genuinely informative for school-finance readers: D districts raise about half the local revenue of A districts, intergovernmental aid closes roughly three-quarters of the gap, and schools located in D polygons then spend somewhat more per pupil than schools in A polygons (\$16,890 vs. an A gap of −\$1,539).
- The literature review is broad and current across HOLC economics, public health, school finance, and desegregation, and the paper includes a section on reasons the relationship might not exist (desegregation, Great Migration, school finance reforms; pp.6–7).

#### Key Concerns

- Figure 3 (p.13) is the wrong figure. Its panels A, B, and D reproduce Figure 4's Percent Black, Percent White, and Simpson's Index series under revenue titles; panel C (0.40–0.83) is consistent with share non-White and matches nothing else in the article; the axes cannot be 2018 dollars given Table 2's \$14,402 total-revenue constant. The longitudinal finance narrative (pp.13–14) and the Discussion's "persistent and growing" claim (p.20) have no displayed support; the coefficients exist only in Supplemental Table A4(A).
- The causal framing outruns the design. The model is a within-CBSA difference in means with no covariates (p.10); HOLC grades recorded neighborhood race, class, and building stock as of the 1930s (p.20); and the revisionist HOLC literature the paper cites (Fishback et al., 2020; Aaronson, Hartley, and Mazumder, 2021; Hillier, 2003; Michney, 2022) finds that the maps explain only a modest share of later differences. Property values, the asserted mechanism for the revenue gap, are never measured. The abstract, introduction, and policy section nonetheless speak of "consequences," "impacts," and policies that "continue to shape" outcomes.
- The prose cannot be trusted for specific numbers. Confirmed text-versus-table errors: Northeast D-school score −0.023 vs. −0.225 (p.18 vs. Table 5); Midwest school PPE gaps of \$302 and \$202 called significant but unstarred (p.14 vs. Table 3); "virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends vs. A/B/C all p<.01 (p.18 vs. Table 5); state/local PPE gaps called "insignificant" (p.20) vs. B −\$1,010* and C −\$745** (Table 3); "smallest between A and C (\$141)" for a D–C contrast of −\$141 (p.14); D districts said to receive more federal revenue than A–C districts (pp.3, 20) when C districts receive \$253 more (p<.01); "across all four Regions" total revenue lower for D districts when West B districts have \$1,082 less (p<.01); "in every Region" D schools more Black and less diverse when West share-Black and Northeast Simpson contrasts are all insignificant (p.21 vs. Table 4). The Table 1 performance sample (5,124 schools) does not match any N in Table 5 (6,890/5,193/6,183), and the Figure 2 legend says 141 CBSAs while its note says 144.
- The Figure 4 time-series text does not match the printed figure. The D–A share-Black gap is described as shrinking from 13.4 to 10.3 points; the plot shows roughly 10 points at both ends. The A–D share-White gap is described as "around 35 percentage points"; the plot shows roughly 27–29. The Simpson's gaps are said to have "surpassed −0.08"; the plot shows roughly 0.05–0.06. The same page says D-school diversity gaps "continued to grow" and, a paragraph later, that D schools are "converging." Whether the quoted numbers come from a fixed-effects specification in Supplemental Table A4(B) is not stated.
- The finance story is internally unresolved and the total-funding claim is fragile. The national A–D and B–D total-revenue gaps are significant only at p<.10 (\$1,546, SE \$822; \$992, SE \$536) and not significant in any region (Table 2); schools in D polygons spend more, not less (Table 3); the Title I explanation cannot account for D schools also having higher state/local spending; and the within-district allocation argument rests on supplemental figures (A6, A7, A10) that do not travel with the article. No school-level model with district fixed effects is reported.
- Inference and measurement are weaker in the regional results. The West has 15 CBSA clusters and the Northeast 30, enrollment weights concentrate influence in a few large districts, no few-cluster correction is reported, and some SEs are implausibly small (Northeast share-Black B coefficient −0.11, SE 0.006). A district enters the sample on any polygon overlap and is graded on the HOLC-covered part of its land area only, so "D district" means "mostly D among its graded area," and the size of the D reference group by region is only in an unavailable supplement.
- Reproducibility is below journal-era norms for a fully-public-data paper: no data or code availability statement, no replication package, no software named, and sample-defining steps that the authors' 2021 working paper documented (NYC sub-districts, point-assigned charter LEAs, dropped E-graded polygons, OLS vs. EB SEDA estimates, race-category count for Simpson's index) are absent from the published article. Mapping Inequality has since moved to a 2023 release with more than 100 additional maps, so a replicator downloading today starts from a different HOLC universe.

#### What to Rely On

- Within the same metro, schools located inside 1930s D-graded polygons today enroll student bodies that are about 36% Black and 14% White nationally (Table 4 constants), and schools in A polygons are 14 points less Black and 30 points more White (Table 4, A rows: −0.14, SE 0.027; 0.30, SE 0.022). The gradient is monotone across grades. Regional exception: in the West, D-polygon schools are 9% Black and the A/B/C share-Black contrasts are all insignificant.
- Schools in D polygons post average math/ELA scores 0.643 SD (SE 0.04) below schools in A polygons nationally, with regional A–D gaps of 0.541–0.753 SD and a monotone gradient (Table 5, first panel). Quote the SD units; the "just over 1.9 grade levels" conversion (p.18) has no stated factor.
- Districts composed mostly of D-graded land raise far less local revenue per pupil: D constant \$5,240 against A–D, B–D, and C–D gaps of \$5,937, \$4,592, and \$1,713, all p<.01 nationally, with the A–D local gap significant in every region (Table 2). State aid offsets much of it (A–D −\$3,670, SE \$752; B–D −\$3,210), and federal aid offsets some (A–D −\$722; B–D −\$391), leaving a net national total-revenue gap of about \$1,546 (p<.10).
- Schools in D polygons have higher nominal per-pupil expenditures than schools in A, B, or C polygons: constant \$16,890 with gaps of −\$1,539 (p<.10), −\$1,313 (p<.05), and −\$882 (p<.01) (Table 3), including higher federal expenditures (−\$602 vs. A, p<.01). The local-revenue shortfall sits at the district level, not in nominal school-level spending.
- Learning rates (within-cohort grade slopes) differ little by HOLC grade nationally (A 0.006, SE 0.006; B 0.008 and C 0.005 at p<.10; Table 5, second panel), so the achievement gap is a gap in levels, consistent with student composition rather than school effectiveness.
- The linkage method itself: area-weighted district grades with cutpoints at 1.5/2.5/3.5 and point-in-polygon school grades (p.10), and the finding that a schools'-average district grade correlates 0.91–0.93 with the area-weighted measure (p.13).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "The consequences of redlining persist today" and any reading of the gaps as effects of the HOLC maps — the design is a no-controls within-metro contrast; the grades recorded pre-existing 1930s conditions; the causal HOLC literature (Aaronson, Hartley, and Mazumder, 2021; Fishback et al., 2020) uses boundary and comparison-city designs precisely because raw grade contrasts are confounded, and finds partial, fading map effects. Cite this paper for description, those papers for causation.
- District finance gaps "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018" (p.20) and everything in the longitudinal finance paragraphs (pp.13–14), including the 2009–10 ARRA spike — the printed Figure 3 is a relabeled copy of the racial-diversity figure and the underlying coefficients (Supplemental Table A4(A)) are not in the article. Unverifiable as published.
- The Figure 4 trend numbers (13.4 to 10.3 points, "around 35 percentage points," gaps "surpassed −0.08") — none can be read off the printed figure, and the page contradicts itself on whether D-school diversity gaps grew or converged. Check Supplemental Table A4(B) before quoting any of them.
- "Districts composed of A to C neighborhoods are better funded" (p.3) — the national total-revenue gaps are p<.10, no regional A–D total gap is significant, West B districts have significantly less than D districts, and schools in D polygons spend more. The robust statement is the local-revenue gap.
- "Districts with D neighborhoods receive more federal Title I funding" (p.3) and federal/state funds "favor D districts relative to A to C districts" (pp.12, 20) — only total federal revenue is observed, and C districts receive \$253 more of it than D districts (p<.01; Table 2). The D–C state difference is insignificant.
- Schools in these areas "predominantly educate Black ... students" (abstract) — 36% nationally, 47–48% in the Midwest and South, 9% in the West (Table 4). "Predominantly non-White and low-income" is supported; "predominantly Black" is not.
- "Virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends (p.18) and the Discussion's "do not reveal whether the gaps have changed over time" (p.21) — the national cohort-trend contrasts are all significant at p<.01 (A 0.010, B 0.007, C 0.004; Table 5) and imply the A–D gap widened across 2009–2018 cohorts, though the magnitudes are small.
- Any specific number quoted from the prose rather than the tables — confirmed slips include −0.023 vs. −0.225 (Northeast), the Midwest \$302/\$202 "significant" claim, the "between A and C (\$141)" label, the p.20 "insignificant" state/local claim, the "across all four Regions" and "in every Region" generalizations, Table 1's 5,124 vs. Table 5's 6,890, and Figure 2's 141 vs. 144.
- Regional estimates, especially the West (15 CBSAs, 159 districts) and South (45 CBSAs, 187 districts) — few clusters, enrollment weighting, no small-sample correction, and many p<.10 stars; re-read the table before citing any regional coefficient.
- The property-value mechanism and the policy implications (decoupling revenue from property taxes, METCO-style transfers, HOLC-based targeting; pp.22–23) — no property-value, assessed-value, or tax-base data are used, no mechanism is tested, and the recommendation of "additional resources" for D-neighborhood schools does not engage Table 3's finding that those schools already spend the most.
- "This article is the first to document the relationship between HOLC grades and modern educational outcomes" (p.22) — the same findings circulated as EdWorkingPaper 21-363 in November 2021 (uncited); Baker, Di Carlo, and Green (2022), cited four times for other purposes, mapped HOLC grades onto district composition and funding adequacy in seven metros; Aaronson et al. (2023), cited on p.5, studied children's educational attainment. Fair as "first national, multi-outcome K–12 analysis."
- Several background citations do not support the claims attached to them — Baker-Smith (2018), a study of suspension policy, for property values in majority-minority neighborhoods (p.20); Hoffman et al. (2020), on urban heat, for property values and demographics (p.2); Baum-Snow and Lutz (2011), on residential location, for causal effects of segregation on school funding and achievement (p.3). The p.2 claim that "most district revenue comes from local sources" is contradicted by p.5 (state 45–47%; property taxes 36%).
- Every robustness check and the FRPL result (79.3% in D schools; A–D −0.37) — all live only in the unavailable supplement (Tables A5–A8, Figures A5–A7, A10); the covariate check in Supplemental Table A7, arguably the most legacy-relevant test in the project, gets one sentence.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a descriptive, within-metro comparison of districts and schools by 1930s HOLC grade. It has no covariates and no identification strategy, and the paper says it is correlational (p.9-10). Its largest cross-sectional contrasts are firmly supported as descriptions: schools in D neighborhoods have lower average test scores, higher Black and lower White shares, and sit in districts that raise less local revenue. The execution and reporting are much weaker than the peer-review stamp suggests. The printed Figure 3 does not show finance data. Several text claims contradict the tables. Table 1's performance sample size does not match Table 5. The abstract and policy sections drift into causal "legacy of redlining" language that the design cannot support. The rating is "Adequate" for the level-gap descriptive findings only. Judged as evidence about redlining's effects, or about how the gaps changed over time, the evidence is weak.

**Strengths:**

- The data are credible, public, and standard: Mapping Inequality HOLC polygons, 2018-19 TIGER district boundaries, NCES EDGE school points, F-33, NERD\$, NCES CCD, and SEDA (p.7-8). Assigning schools by point-in-polygon (p.10) is transparent and easy to replicate.
- CBSA fixed effects keep every comparison within a metro area. This removes the most obvious confound, which is cross-metro differences in cost, state finance systems, and demographics.
- The headline level gaps are large, precisely estimated, and consistent across regions. Examples: average test scores, A vs D, 0.643 SD (SE 0.04) nationally and 0.541-0.753 SD in all four regions (p.19, Table 5, avg. math and ELA row A). Share White, A vs D, 0.30 (SE 0.022), with every regional A coefficient at 0.27-0.33 (p.16, Table 4, % White row A). Local revenue per pupil, A vs D, \$5937 (SE \$1228), significant in every region (p.12, Table 2, PPR local row A).
- Table 2 adds up internally. The federal, state, and local coefficients sum to the total-revenue coefficients: for example, the Overall A row gives −722 − 3670 + 5937 = 1545 against a printed \$1546, and the West B row gives −298 − 2557 + 1773 = −1082 against a printed −\$1082 (p.12, Table 2). Table 2 Ns are consistent with Table 1 (1760 districts; regional Ns 806+608+187+159 = 1760), and so are Table 3 Ns (9023 = 2744+3466+1340+1473) and Table 4 Ns (9709 = 3031+3595+1453+1630).
- The paper reports several sensitivity checks that bear on the right questions: a non-discretized grade and a school-average grade (p.12-13), panel-only samples (p.19, Supp. Table A5), results without CBSA fixed effects (Supp. Table A6), and covariates (Supp. Table A7). None of these could be checked, because the supplement was unavailable.

**Weaknesses:**

- [checkable] **The printed Figure 3 is the wrong figure.** Its panels are titled per-pupil total, federal, state, and local revenue "(USD 2018)", but the y-axes run from about 0.20 to 0.85. Panels A, B, and D are point-for-point identical to Figure 4's % Black, % White, and Simpson's Index panels (compare p.13, Figure 3 with p.17, Figure 4). Panel C equals 1 − % White, i.e., the share non-White (for example, D ≈ 0.70 in 1988-89 against % White D ≈ 0.30). As a result, the paper has no displayed evidence for its district-finance time-series claims. Those claims include "an initial and subsequently increasing gap" (p.13-14), the 2009-10 ARRA federal "spike" (p.14), which could not appear on a figure with four decadal points anyway, and the Discussion's "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018" (p.20). The paper says the coefficients are in Supp. Table A4(A), which could not be checked.
- [checkable] **The text describing Figure 4 does not match the printed Figure 4** (p.17-18 text vs p.17, Figure 4, read from the rendered figure):
  - The D−A gap in % Black is described as falling from 13.4 to 10.3 pp. The plotted gap is about 10 pp in both 1988-89 and 2018-19.
  - The D−A gap in % White is described as "around 35 percentage points". The plotted gap is about 25-29 pp.
  - The Simpson gaps for D vs A and B are said to have "surpassed −0.08" by 2018-19. The plotted gaps are about 0.05-0.06.
  - C schools are described as "remaining flat" on Simpson's Index. The plotted C line rises from about 0.37 to about 0.46.
  - The same page also contradicts itself on Simpson's Index. D-school gaps "continued to grow" in one sentence; a paragraph later, D schools were "converging toward" A-C trajectories (both p.18).
- [checkable] **The performance sample size in Table 1 does not match Table 5.** Table 1 gives 5124 SEDA schools (p.9, Table 1, Student performance column). Table 5 reports N = 6890 for average scores, 5193 for learning rates, and 6183 for test-score change (p.19, Table 5, N rows). All three exceed 5124, and none equals it.
- [checkable] **Test-score trends are misreported.** The text says there are "virtually no statistically significant differences" nationally in learning rates and test-score trends (p.18). Yet every national trend coefficient is significant at p<.01: A 0.01 (0.003), B 0.007 (0.002), C 0.004 (0.001) (p.19, Table 5, Avg. student test score change, Overall). The next paragraph discusses these same coefficients. The Discussion then says the performance results "do not reveal whether the gaps have changed over time" (p.21), and p.11 says time-series data are "unavailable" for performance. But SEDA's cohort trend measure is exactly a 2009-2018 change measure. Its positive A-C coefficients mean the A-D gap widened across cohorts.
- [checkable] **Other text-vs-table errors, each confirmed on the rendered page:**
  - Midwest school PPE. The text says A (\$302) and B (\$202) neighborhoods have "statistically significant higher spending" (p.14). Both are insignificant: \$302 (\$555) and \$202 (\$630) (p.15, Table 3, PPE total, Midwest).
  - The Northeast D-school average score is printed as −0.023 SD in the text (p.18). The table shows −0.225 (0.021) (p.19, Table 5, Constant, Northeast).
  - The smallest federal-expenditure gap is described as "between A and C (\$141)" (p.14). The table entry is C vs D, −\$141 (p.15, Table 3, PPE federal, C).
  - The text says the D-C federal-revenue gap is insignificant only in the Northeast and South (p.11). The West is also insignificant: \$182 (\$151) (p.12, Table 2).
- [checkable] **Headline summaries overstate the tables.**
  - The Discussion says D districts "receive higher per-pupil federal and state revenues than districts with A to C neighborhoods" (p.20), and p.3 says the same about federal Title I funding. But C districts receive more federal revenue than D districts: \$253 (SE \$76), p<.01 (p.12, Table 2, PPR federal, Overall C). The D-vs-C state difference is insignificant: −\$461 (\$495).
  - The Discussion says D-school state/local expenditure differences are "insignificant" (p.20). Table 3 shows B −\$1010* (\$590) and C −\$745** (\$323) (p.15), and the Results text itself calls them significant (p.14).
  - The p.11 claim that total PPR is lower for D districts "across all four Regions" fails in the West, where B districts have less revenue than D districts: −\$1082 (\$307), p<.01 (p.12, Table 2).
  - The Discussion says that "in every Region" D schools have higher Black shares and less diverse student bodies (p.21). The West % Black contrasts are all insignificant, with F = 0.22 (p.16, Table 4). The Northeast Simpson contrasts are all insignificant: 0.04, 0.02, 0.01 (p.16, Table 4).
- [checkable] **The national total-revenue gap is only marginally significant.** The A and B coefficients are significant only at p<.10: \$1546 (\$822) and \$992 (\$536) (p.12, Table 2, PPR total, Overall). The text reports them simply as "statistically significant" (p.11), and the national D-vs-A total PPE gap is treated the same way: −\$1539 (\$852), p<.10 (p.15, Table 3). The claim that districts made up of A-C neighborhoods are "better funded" overall (p.3) rests on these estimates.
- [checkable] **The weighting described in Methods differs from the weighting in Table 5.** Methods says all outcomes are weighted by enrollment (p.10). The Table 5 note says the models are weighted by the number of math and ELA tests (p.19).
- [judgment] **The district grade is a noisy measure of a district's historical neighborhood makeup.**
  - The grade is an average over the HOLC-covered part of the district only (p.10). A district that touches a single 1930s polygon enters the sample and is graded by that sliver. Meanwhile, the regression weight is the district's total enrollment, most of which may live on ungraded land.
  - Land area is a poor proxy for residents or parcels. Low-density A/B areas and large industrial D areas carry weight out of proportion to their populations.
  - The unequal bins (A 1-1.5, B 1.5-2.5, C 2.5-3.5, D 3.5-4; p.10) leave A and D as thin tails. The size of the D reference group, especially in the South (187 districts in 45 CBSAs) and West (159 districts in 15 CBSAs) (p.12, Table 2; p.8, Figure 2 note), is only in Supp. Table A1, which could not be checked. If the D group is small, every district contrast depends on a few districts.
  - Enrollment weighting makes this worse. A few very large urban districts can dominate a regional coefficient, and no unweighted or leave-one-out results are reported in the main text.
- [judgment] **Inference in the regional samples is fragile.** CBSA-clustered standard errors are reasonable nationally (144 clusters). The West has 15 clusters and the Northeast 30 (p.8, Figure 2 note), with very unequal cluster sizes once enrollment weights are applied. Conventional cluster-robust SEs tend to be too small in that setting, and some are implausibly small, e.g., Northeast % Black B −0.11 (0.006) (p.16, Table 4). No small-sample correction or wild-cluster bootstrap is reported. Across 4 finance, 3 PPE, 3 diversity, and 3 performance outcomes × 5 samples × 3 contrasts, there are many tests with no multiplicity adjustment, and many regional stars are at p<.10.
- [judgment] **The paper does not really reconcile the district and school finance results.**
  - The district-level revenue results are F-33 revenue for 2017-18, which includes capital and debt revenue. The school-level results are NERD\$ site-level expenditures for 2018-19, a state-reported measure whose allocation of central costs differs across states (p.7, 14). These measure different things, in different years, on different samples.
  - The paper's Title I explanation cannot account for D schools also having higher state/local spending (p.15, Table 3). Regressing FRPL share on HOLC grade (p.14-15) shows that D schools are poorer. It does not show how funds are allocated within districts.
  - The direct test would be a school-level model with district fixed effects, and none is reported. The claim that A-C districts "direct more resources to their schools in D neighborhoods" (p.15) rests on Supp. Figures A6/A7, which could not be checked.
- [judgment] **The design cannot separate an effect of redlining from what HOLC graded.** HOLC grades encoded neighborhood race, class, and housing stock as they already were in the 1930s (p.4, p.20). A raw within-CBSA contrast therefore measures how persistent those neighborhood conditions have been, plus whatever the maps added. The paper uses none of the designs it surveys on p.8-9, such as boundary discontinuities or comparisons with ungraded or below-threshold cities. The property-value mechanism is inferred from the literature, not measured; no assessed-value data are used.
  - The covariate check with 1930s-era family income, % Black, and building age (Supp. Table A7, p.20) is the only relevant evidence, and it could not be checked.
  - Even so, the abstract says "the consequences of redlining persist today" and that historic policies "continue to shape educational outcomes" (p.1). Page 3 asserts a "because" mechanism for Title I. The policy section speaks of "redlining's impacts" and "redlining's impact on neighborhood demographic stratification" (p.22). These phrases sit alongside disclaimers of causality elsewhere (p.9-10, p.21).
- [judgment] **The SEDA conversions are unexplained.** The 0.64 SD ≈ "just over 1.9 grade levels" conversion (p.18) implies about 0.34 SD per grade, and neither the factor nor its source is given. The paper uses SEDA's CS scale, in which a grade-level interpretation is only approximate and varies by grade. At that factor, the largest significant learning-rate contrast, 0.023 (0.009) for the Northeast A row (p.19, Table 5), is about 1/15 of a grade per grade. That does not match "just over 1/20th" (p.18). The paper also does not say that these slopes accumulate over grades 3-8.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the national cross-sectional **level gaps** as descriptions: test scores (0.64 SD A vs D; p.19, Table 5), racial composition (p.16, Table 4, % Black and % White), and district local revenue (p.12, Table 2). They are large, consistent across regions, and unlikely to be overturned by the measurement and inference issues above. Read them as "D-graded parts of 1930s cities today house poorer, more Black, lower-scoring schools and lower-tax-base districts." Do not read them as effects of the HOLC maps.
- Do not cite the district **finance time-series** findings (increasing total and local gaps since 1989, the ARRA spike; p.13-14, p.20). The figure printed as their evidence is a racial-composition figure, and the underlying coefficients are only in an unchecked supplement.
- Treat the **total-funding** claim ("A-C districts are better funded") as suggestive only: its national estimates are significant at p<.10 (p.12, Table 2), and schools in D neighborhoods actually **spend more** per pupil (p.15, Table 3). Reliable statements are narrower: D districts raise much less local revenue and receive more state aid than A/B districts. On federal revenue, D districts receive more than A/B districts but less than C districts.
- Before citing any single **regional** estimate, especially for the West (15 CBSAs) or Northeast (30), re-read the table yourself. The text misstates several regional results, and few-cluster standard errors are probably too small. Treat p<.10 regional stars as noise.
- On achievement, the gap is in **levels**, not growth. Learning-rate differences are small and mostly insignificant (p.19, Table 5), which fits the idea that the gap reflects what students bring to school more than school effectiveness. The cohort-trend coefficients do indicate that the A-D gap **widened** from 2009 to 2018, despite the Discussion's statement that change over time is unknown (p.21).
- Check the table, not the prose, for any specific number. Several confirmed mismatches exist (Northeast −0.225 vs "−0.023"; Midwest PPE "significant" vs insignificant; the Figure 4 gap magnitudes). The Table 1 vs Table 5 sample-size discrepancy means readers cannot be sure which SEDA sample underlies Table 5.
- Treat the **policy implications** as hypotheses motivated by the literature, not conclusions from this analysis. They include decoupling revenue from property taxes and expanding enrollment options (p.22). The paper does not measure property values, test mechanisms, or estimate any causal effect.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and what it can support.* The model is an enrollment-weighted regression of each outcome on A, B, and C indicators, with D as the omitted category, CBSA fixed effects, no covariates, and CBSA-clustered SEs (p.10). In effect, it is a within-metro difference in means. For the stated question of whether 1930s grades still line up with today's educational patterns, that is a sensible and transparent tool, and the paper sometimes frames its contribution correctly ("the ability to predict current educational outcomes... is compelling", p.22). The problem is that HOLC grades were not assigned at random. By design, they recorded existing racial composition, class, and building age (p.4, p.20), so a D-vs-A contrast bundles pre-existing 1930s differences with any later effect of the maps and the lending patterns they shaped. The HOLC literature the authors cite handles this with boundary designs or comparisons with ungraded or below-threshold cities (p.8-9). None is used here. The "legacy" and "consequences" language in the title, abstract, and policy section therefore goes further than the design allows. The p.9-10 and p.21 disclaimers are accurate but sit uneasily beside it.

*Measurement of exposure.* The school assignment is clean: a school gets the grade of the polygon containing it (p.10). Two limits follow. Schools outside the 1930s city footprint are dropped, so the school sample describes the historical urban core only. And a school's location stands in for its students' neighborhoods, which is weaker for magnet, charter, or choice schools; the paper does not say whether these are included. The district measure is more problematic. It averages grades over the HOLC-covered part of the district, weighted by land area (p.10), and a district enters with any intersection. A large suburban district whose edge touches an old A polygon therefore becomes an "A district" and carries its full enrollment weight. This measurement error is not classical: it probably pushes suburban districts toward A/B and central-city districts toward C/D, so the district contrasts are partly city-versus-suburb contrasts. The reported agreement with a school-based district grade (r = 0.93 raw, 0.91 discretized; p.13) is reassuring, but it covers only districts with schools inside polygons, and the binned scatterplots behind it (Supp. Fig. A5) could not be checked. The unequal bin widths are a defensible nearest-integer choice. Even so, the number of districts in the D reference group, which every district coefficient depends on, is not in the main text.

*Inference.* Clustering by CBSA is the right level. With 144 clusters the national SEs are probably fine. The regional models are another matter: the West has 15 clusters and the Northeast 30 (p.8), enrollment weights concentrate influence in a few large systems, and no few-cluster correction is reported. Some SEs look implausibly small, such as Northeast % Black B −0.11 (0.006) and the Northeast Simpson constant 0.5 (0.002) (p.16, Table 4). In the text, "statistically significant" covers p<.10 results without saying so, and the headline national total-funding contrasts are among them (p.12, Table 2). The "percent differences" in the text divide by the regression constant (for example, "10%" = 1546/14,402 on p.11). With CBSA fixed effects, that constant is only an approximation of the D-group mean.

*District revenue vs school expenditure.* The two finance levels point in opposite directions. D districts have lower total revenue (p.12, Table 2), but schools in D neighborhoods have higher total expenditures, \$16,890 against A −\$1539 (p.15, Table 3). The paper's reconciliation is thin (p.14-15):

- An aggregation exercise and supplemental figures that could not be checked.
- An FRPL regression that shows D schools are poorer but says nothing about how districts allocate funds.
- A Title I story that cannot explain why D schools also have higher state/local spending (B and C significant; p.15, Table 3).

Other explanations are at least as plausible: revenue vs expenditure (capital and debt), 2017-18 vs 2018-19, the F-33 vs NERD\$ accounting differences across states, and the fact that D-neighborhood schools mostly sit inside large central-city districts that also contain A-C schools. A school-level model with district fixed effects would have settled the within-district allocation question. Readers should treat "who is better funded" as unresolved, not reconciled.

*Time series.* The finance time series (1109 districts, 143 CBSAs; p.9, Table 1) and the diversity time series (4677 schools, 118 CBSAs; p.9, Table 1; p.17) use reduced, apparently balanced panels. The figure notes (p.13, p.17) do not say whether CBSA fixed effects are included, they differ on whether the regressors are "A to D" or "A to C" indicators, and they show no confidence intervals despite mentioning clustered SEs. Most seriously, the printed Figure 3 duplicates the racial-composition series, so the finance-trend narrative has no displayed support. The Figure 4 text also disagrees with the printed Figure 4 on several magnitudes (listed above). The 2018-19 panel values also differ noticeably from the cross-section: the plotted D−A % Black gap is about 10 pp against 0.14 in Table 4 (p.16). That may reflect the panel restriction, or the absence of fixed effects in the figure, and it sits oddly with the claim of "no meaningful differences" (p.19, Supp. Table A5(B), which could not be checked). Taken together, the reporting errors in this section suggest the exhibits and text drifted apart across revisions. Readers should rely on the time-series claims least of anything in the paper.

*SEDA outcomes.* The outcome definitions (p.8) match SEDA's school-level pooled means, grade slopes (learning rates), and cohort slopes (trends) on the CS scale. The pooled mean is mainly a measure of student composition, so the large A-D level gap is expected given Table 4 and the FRPL gradient (p.14-15). The learning-rate results are more informative about schools, and they show little difference by grade (p.19, Table 5). The paper undersells a genuine dynamic finding and then contradicts itself about it. The cohort-trend coefficients are all significant nationally and imply a widening A-D gap over 2009-2018, yet the text calls them "virtually no" significant differences (p.18) and later says change over time is unknown (p.21). The unexplained grade-level conversion and the Table 1/Table 5 sample-size mismatch are further signs of loose execution.

*Bottom line.* The central descriptive picture holds up, and it is useful: within the same metros, schools and districts in formerly D-graded areas today are poorer, more segregated, lower-scoring, and more dependent on state aid. Readers can cite those level gaps with confidence as descriptions. Much of the rest should be discounted: the time trends in finance and diversity, the "better funded overall" claim, most regional nuance, the district/school funding reconciliation, and any reading of these gaps as effects of redlining. The density of confirmed text-exhibit errors, including a wrong figure, is unusual for a published article and should lower readers' trust in any detail not visible in Tables 2-5.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper cites widely and sensibly across the HOLC economics, public-health, school-finance, and desegregation literatures, and it deserves credit for a dedicated section on reasons the relationship might have faded (pp.6-7). Its account of prior work is less reliable than its breadth suggests. It cites the key revisionist HOLC studies (Fishback et al., 2020; Hillier, 2003; Michney, 2022; Aaronson, Hartley, & Mazumder, 2021) for background facts but never engages their central finding: HOLC grades largely recorded neighborhood differences that already existed. Several citations do not support the claims attached to them. The "first to document" claim (p.22) holds for the paper's national scope, but it is worded more broadly than that, and it leaves out the authors' own 2021 working paper and a 2022 HOLC-to-school-funding analysis that the paper cites for other purposes.

**Strengths:**

- The paper draws on a genuinely interdisciplinary set of sources: the economics of HOLC (Aaronson, Hartley, & Mazumder, 2021; Aaronson et al., 2023; Anders, 2023; Appel & Nickerson, 2016; Krimmel, 2018), sociology and geography (Faber, 2021; Graetz & Esposito, 2023; Markley, 2021), public health (Beard et al., 2017; Jacoby et al., 2018; Nardone et al., 2020), and environmental research (Hoffman et al., 2020; Salazar-Miranda et al., 2024) (pp.2-5, p.9).
- School-finance coverage is current and strong: Jackson, Johnson, & Persico (2016), Lafortune et al. (2018), Biasi (2023), Hoxby (2001), Card & Payne (2002), Shores et al. (2022), Jackson & Mackevicius (2024), and Baron et al. (2024) (pp.5-7, p.21). The paper also correctly uses Gordon & Reber (2022, 2023) to explain why school-level and district-level finance results diverge (p.20).
- The segregation and desegregation literature is well represented: Reardon et al. (2012), Lutz (2011), Liebowitz (2018), Liebowitz & Page (2014), Baum-Snow & Lutz (2011), Cascio et al. (2008), Boustan (2010, 2012), Fiel (2013), Owens (2016, 2020), Rich et al. (2021), and Monarrez et al. (2022) (pp.6-7).
- Some readers will not know the full range of HOLC research designs. The methods section usefully surveys them (within-city ungraded comparisons, the 40,000-population threshold, boundary designs, and polygon-average comparisons), and it places this paper among the descriptive polygon-average studies (pp.8-9).
- A section titled "Potential Reasons the HOLC and Contemporary Education Outcomes Relationship May Not Exist" (pp.6-7) sets up a real test against desegregation and school finance reform. Few persistence papers in education do this.

**Weaknesses:**

- [checkable] **The paper cites the revisionist HOLC literature but does not engage its main finding.** Fishback et al. (2020) is cited on p.4 and p.9 only for HOLC's refinancing role and for interpreting grades. By my web check of the NBER abstract, that study concludes that racial bias in the maps explains "at most 4 to 20 percent" of Black households' concentration in D zones; decades of earlier discrimination had already placed them there. Aaronson, Hartley, & Mazumder (2021) is cited as showing that redlining shaped segregation and property values (p.3, p.5). Its working-paper version (verified) says the maps account for 15-30% of the D-C gap in share Black and in homeownership, and 40% of the gap in house values, from 1950 to 1980, with many estimates waning after 1970. Hillier (2003) and Michney (2022) are cited only for descriptive facts (p.4, p.9, p.20). The paper's A-versus-D contrasts therefore mostly measure differences that predate the maps. The literature it cites says so, but the text never tells the reader.
- [judgment] **The framing is more causal than the cited evidence supports.** The paper says it takes a "more conservative correlational approach" (p.9) and calls the grades a "proxy" for 1930s neighborhood traits (p.20). Yet the abstract says "the consequences of redlining persist today" (p.1). The introduction says "redlining prevented predominantly middle-class Black families from purchasing property," citing an NCRC report, a dataset, and a history of the Federal Home Loan Bank Board rather than causal studies (p.2). The policy section speaks of "redlining's impacts on property values" (p.22). The definition on p.2 ("mortgage lenders drawing red lines on maps") also runs together private lending discrimination and HOLC's appraisal maps, a distinction the historiography the paper cites takes care to keep.
- [checkable] **Key revisionist and sociological HOLC work is missing from the reference list:**
  - Fishback, Rose, Snowden, & Storrs, "New Evidence on Redlining by Federal Housing Programs in the 1930s" (J. Urban Economics, 2024; verified). FHA exclusion predated the maps, and HOLC lent broadly in D areas.
  - Hillier (2005, Social Science History; verified). In Philadelphia, lenders avoided red areas before the maps existed, and the maps were not widely distributed.
  - Michney & Winling (2020, J. Urban History; verified). HOLC made loans to Black borrowers.
  - Faber (2020, American Sociological Review, "We Built This"; verified). This is the main sociology study of HOLC and city-level segregation; the paper cites only Faber (2021).
  - Rutan & Glass (2018, Professional Geographer, "The Lingering Effects of Neighborhood Appraisal"; verified). An earlier HOLC persistence study with a near-identical title.
- [checkable] **Several citations do not support the claims attached to them:**
  - p.20: Baker-Smith (2018) is cited for the claim that majority-minority neighborhoods have lower property values. The reference title and abstract (verified) are about high school suspension-policy changes.
  - p.2: Hoffman et al. (2020) is cited for lower property values and concentrations of people of color and poverty in D neighborhoods. It is a study of urban heat exposure.
  - p.3: Baum-Snow & Lutz (2011) is cited among works showing "well-documented causal effects" of segregation and property values on school funding and achievement. It studies how desegregation affected where families lived.
  - p.3 and p.20: Acharya, Blackwell, & Sen (2016a) is cited as historical-persistence literature. By my recollection, not verified here, it is a methods paper on estimating controlled direct effects.
- [checkable] **Bayer, Blair, & Whaley (2020) is cited correctly on p.5 but misdescribed on p.6.** The NBER abstract (verified) says the paper tests efficiency through the effect of salary spending and taxes on house prices, so it is a legitimate capitalization citation on p.5. On p.6, the sentence it supports reverses the direction of capitalization: "increases in housing taxes are often directly capitalized into school spending." In that literature, school spending and taxes are capitalized into house prices.
- [checkable] **Some descriptive facts are internally inconsistent or overstated.**
  - p.2 says "most district revenue comes from local sources." p.5 says state funding is 45-47% and property taxes 36%.
  - p.5 says Title I and IDEA "together account for 8% to 11%" of revenue. NCES reports that all federal revenue was 8% in 2017-18 (verified), so these two programs alone must be less.
  - p.7 calls the SFRs "local court-ordered"; they were state court orders.
- [checkable] **Reference-list errors.** Jackson, Wigger, & Xiong (2018) is listed as "National Bureau of Economic Research, 13(2), 10-21" with the NBER w24203 DOI (p.26). The published version is AEJ: Economic Policy 13(2): 304-335 (2021) (verified). Markley is dated 2021 but listed with a 2023 journal volume and an OSF preprint DOI.
- [checkable] **The "first to document" claim (p.22; see also p.20, "this effort has yet to extend to modern educational outcomes") is imprecise.**
  - The authors' own EdWorkingPaper 21-363 (Lukes & Cleveland, November 2021; verified) is not cited.
  - Baker, Di Carlo, & Green (2022, Shanker Institute; verified) mapped HOLC grades onto district racial composition, school-neighborhood poverty, and cost-adjusted funding adequacy in seven metros. The paper cites it four times (pp.2, 5, 6, 20), but only for general school-finance claims.
  - Other HOLC-education work also exists: Jung et al. (2022, Environment International; verified) on air pollution near NYC schools, and DeAngelis et al. (2024, Population Research and Policy Review; verified) on college completion in the Add Health cohort. Powers & Ross (Urban Education, in press 2026; verified) on Oakland school segregation is contemporaneous.
  - The priority claim is fair only as "first national, multi-outcome K-12 analysis."
- [judgment] **The persistence framing is mostly decorative.** Cirone & Pepinsky (2022) is cited as support for the paper's own empirical finding (p.3) and in the Figure 1 note (p.4). The mechanisms, the "missing middle" between the 1930s and today, and the decomposition tools this literature emphasizes are not used, including those in the Acharya et al. (2016a) paper it cites. The paper also omits the main methodological critique of persistence regressions, Kelly's "The Standard Errors of Persistence" (J. International Economics, 2025; verified). Its spatial-noise argument applies directly to school-level outcomes grouped within metro areas.
- [judgment] **Evidence that cuts against the narrative is only partly engaged.**
  - The paper does not connect its own convergence result (the D-A gap in % Black shrinks from 13.4 to 10.3 percentage points, p.17) to Aaronson et al.'s finding that effects wane after 1970, or to post-Fair Housing Act declines in segregation.
  - It does not discuss gentrification of formerly D-graded areas. NCRC's 2019 "Shifting Neighborhoods" report (verified) links gentrification to greater economic change in "Hazardous" areas, and the paper's own source (Mitchell & Franco, 2018) implies that about one in four D areas is no longer struggling.
  - State aid strongly favors D districts (\$3,670 more per pupil than A districts, Table 2, pp.11-12). That is evidence that equalization worked in part, but the paper presents the remaining gap as persisting "despite" reform (p.21) without engaging the cost-adjusted adequacy literature. That literature determines whether a roughly 10% unadjusted revenue gap (p.11) is large.
- [checkable] **Relevant school-segregation and school-finance work is omitted.**
  - Monarrez (2023, AEJ: Applied; verified) finds that residential segregation explains more than 100% of school segregation and that attendance boundaries slightly integrate schools. This bears directly on the paper's "neighborhood-oriented enrollment" channel.
  - Sosina & Weathers (2019, AERA Open; verified) covers between-district segregation and spending disparities.
  - EdBuild's 2019 "\$23 billion" report (verified) found a funding gap by district racial composition. Its founder, Rebecca Sibilia, is thanked in the acknowledgments; that she founded EdBuild is from my recollection.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- For a causal reading of what HOLC maps did, read Aaronson, Hartley, & Mazumder (2021, AEJ: Policy) and Fishback et al. (2020, NBER w28146) alongside this paper. Together they imply that most of the A-D gaps reported here reflect conditions that predate the maps. Cite this paper for descriptive patterns, not for effects of redlining.
- For the historiography that the paper cites but does not engage, read Hillier (2003, 2005), Michney & Winling (2020), and Fishback, Rose, Snowden, & Storrs (2024, J. Urban Economics).
- On priority: cite Lukes & Cleveland (2021, EdWorkingPaper 21-363) as the first public version of this national analysis. Cite Baker, Di Carlo, & Green (2022, Shanker Institute) as a parallel seven-metro HOLC-to-district study that uses cost-adjusted adequacy measures instead of raw per-pupil revenue. Do not repeat the p.22 "first to document" claim without that qualification.
- Do not repeat these citations without checking them: Baker-Smith (2018) for property values (p.20); Hoffman et al. (2020) for property values and demographics (p.2); Baum-Snow & Lutz (2011) for causal effects on school funding and achievement (p.3); the p.5 statement that Title I and IDEA are 8-11% of revenue; and the p.2 statement that most revenue is local.
- For the school-assignment channel, Monarrez (2023) and Reardon et al. (2012) are better anchors than the paper's own reasoning. Monarrez implies that most of the school gaps here come through residential sorting, not attendance-zone design.
- For whether persistence regressions of this kind are robust, read Kelly (2025, "The Standard Errors of Persistence") before treating the uniformly significant regional estimates as strong evidence of persistence.
- For evidence that runs against a simple persistence story, see Pearman (2019, Review of Educational Research) on gentrification and achievement, and the post-1970 convergence in Aaronson et al. (2021). Both matter for reading the time-series figures (pp.13-18).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What I verified versus what I recall.* I checked the following by web lookup: the existence and content of the EdWorkingPaper 21-363 version; Baker, Di Carlo, & Green (2022) and its HOLC analysis; Fishback et al. (2020), its 4-20% finding; the Aaronson, Hartley, & Mazumder working-paper statements (15-30% and 40%, waning after 1970); Fishback, Rose, Snowden, & Storrs (2024); Hillier (2005); Michney & Winling (2020); Faber (2020); Rutan & Glass (2018); the Bayer, Blair, & Whaley abstract; the Baker-Smith abstract; the published citation for Jackson, Wigger, & Xiong; the NCES 8% federal share; Kelly (2025); Monarrez (2023); Sosina & Weathers (2019); Pearman (2019); NCRC (2019); Jung et al. (2022); DeAngelis et al. (2024); and Powers & Ross (2026). The following are from my recollection and were not re-checked: the content of Acharya et al. (2016a); how Cirone & Pepinsky (2022) treat mechanisms; and Rebecca Sibilia's role at EdBuild. The supplemental material was not available to me, so I cannot judge whether the appendix engages any of the omitted work.

*The central problem.* The paper's biggest literature weakness is not a missing citation. It is how it handles work it already cites. The HOLC literature since about 2017 has had to answer one question: did the maps change neighborhoods, or did they record differences that already existed? The strongest causal work (Aaronson, Hartley, & Mazumder, 2021) finds real but partial effects that were concentrated at boundaries and faded after 1970. Fishback et al. (2020) find that the maps' racial bias explains a small share of Black concentration in D zones. Both are in the reference list, and both are used only for background. Meanwhile, the paper's design compares whole A polygons with whole D polygons within CBSAs (pp.9-10). By the logic of that literature, this design captures the full pre-1935 gradient plus whatever the maps added. The paper partly acknowledges this: on p.9 and p.20 it says the grades proxy for 1930s neighborhood characteristics. That is the more accurate reading. Readers should take that reading and not the causal language of the abstract, the title, and the policy section.

*School finance.* The school-finance review is the strongest part of the paper. The claim that the gaps survive "despite" SFRs (p.21) is fair as a description. But the fuller literature supports a more balanced reading of the paper's own tables. State and federal aid is clearly progressive with respect to HOLC grade (Table 2). The remaining total-revenue gap is about 7-10% (p.11) before any cost adjustment. The adequacy framework in Baker et al. (2022), a report the paper cites, is the standard way to judge whether that gap is large relative to need. The internal inconsistencies (p.2 versus p.5 on revenue shares, and the 8-11% figure for Title I and IDEA) are small, but they should make readers cautious about repeating the paper's background facts without checking.

*Novelty.* The paper's real contribution is a national, 144-CBSA descriptive analysis that covers funding, composition, and achievement in one design. The authors first circulated it in 2021, before most comparable work, so they have a legitimate priority claim for that scope. But the sentence on p.22 claims more than that. It omits the authors' own working paper. It also omits the HOLC analysis in Baker et al. (2022), which the paper cites four times for other purposes. And the paper itself cites Aaronson et al. (2023) on educational attainment (p.5, p.22). Readers should cite this paper for national descriptive magnitudes. They should cite Baker et al. (2022) for metro case studies with adequacy-adjusted funding, and the Aaronson and Fishback papers for how much of the gap the maps themselves caused.

*Place in the field.* The paper sits between the economics of historical persistence and the education-policy literature on segregation and school finance. It uses the first mostly as framing: Cirone & Pepinsky and Acharya et al. appear at the start and end and are not otherwise used. It uses the second more substantively. Two ideas from economics would change how the findings read. First, spatial-autocorrelation critiques (Kelly, 2025) suggest caution about uniformly significant persistence estimates. Second, the post-1970 convergence documented by Aaronson et al. matches the paper's own shrinking D-A gap in % Black (p.17), which the discussion instead ties to resegregation (p.21). From sociology and education research, the gentrification literature (Pearman, 2019) and work on attendance boundaries (Monarrez, 2023) supply the mechanisms that the conceptual framework (Figure 1, p.4) says are "ensured" but that the paper does not test.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper's skeleton is easy to follow: three outcome families, each with a cross-sectional table and, for two of them, a time-series figure. The core cross-sectional coefficients in Tables 2–5 are mostly quoted correctly. But the printed Figure 3 (district revenue trends) is not a revenue figure: three of its four panels are the Figure 4 racial-diversity plots with new titles. That leaves the paper's "persistent and growing" finance-trend claim with no visible exhibit behind it. On top of that, the results prose, the Discussion and the abstract contain a string of confirmed text-versus-table errors, the paper overgeneralizes about its regional results, and its causal language drifts beyond what its stated correlational design supports. A reader should trust the tables over the prose throughout.

**Strengths:**

- The organization is clear and predictable. The research questions (p2) map one-to-one onto the Results subsections (p11–19), and each subsection moves from "Current Outcomes" to "Longitudinal Outcomes" in the same order.
- Tables 2–5 share one layout (Overall plus four Census Regions; A/B/C coefficients against a D reference; constant = D-group mean; N, R², F). Every table note states the reference category, weighting, fixed effects and clustering. Once a reader learns one table, they can read all four.
- Most headline cross-sectional numbers in the prose match the tables exactly: district total/federal/state/local PPR constants and D–A gaps (p11 vs p12 Table 2), the school PPE constant and overall gaps (p14 vs p15 Table 3), the national % Black and Simpson's figures (p16 vs p16 Table 4), and the national D–A test-score gap of 0.643 SD (p18 vs p19 Table 5).
- The regional Ns sum exactly to the overall Ns in every panel of Tables 2–5 (for example, p12 Table 2: 806+608+187+159 = 1760; p15 Table 3 PPE total: 2744+3466+1340+1473 = 9023; p16 Table 4: 9709). The Table 1 counts for finance and diversity (p9) match Tables 2–4.
- The Methods section says plainly that the design is a "conservative correlational approach" (p9–10), and the Discussion repeats "this article's results are not causal" (p21).
- Supplemental cross-references are internally consistent: Tables A1–A8 and Figures A1–A12 are each cited, and the endnotes (p23) point to the margins plots or coefficient tables for each main exhibit.

**Weaknesses:**

- [checkable] Figure 3 (p13, "District per-pupil revenue by HOLC grade ... (USD 2018)") is the wrong image. Panels A ("Per-Pupil Total Revenue"), B ("Federal") and D ("Local") have exactly the same markers, values and y-axes as Figure 4 (p17) Panels A (% Black), B (% White) and C (Simpson's Index). Panel C ("State") is the only unique panel, and its y-axis (0.40–0.83) carries no dollar units. The x-axis runs to 2018–2019, a year the F-33 data (1989–90 to 2017–18, p7) does not cover. All of the p13–14 longitudinal finance prose, and the Discussion's claim that district finance gaps are "persistent and growing over time" (p20), therefore rest on an exhibit the reader cannot see. The underlying numbers are only in Supplemental Table A4(A) (endnote 3).
- [checkable] The p14 prose on Figure 3 also contradicts the printed panels. It describes a gap "that favors A to C districts" in total revenue (Panel A shows D highest), large initial local-revenue gaps in the late 1980s (Panel D shows near-zero gaps), federal revenue favoring C/D (Panel B shows D lowest), and a "large positive spike ... for 2009–2010" (the figure has only decade points: 1988–89, 1998–99, 2008–09, 2018–19).
- [checkable] Several results sentences misstate the table: significance in the Midwest PPE row, a mislabeled and sign-flipped federal PPE comparison, a Northeast test-score constant off by a factor of 10, and a "virtually no significant differences" claim contradicted by three significant coefficients (items 3–6 of the audit below).
- [checkable] The Discussion restates results more strongly or differently than the Results section and tables do: state/local PPE differences called "insignificant" (two of three are significant), D-neighborhood diversity patterns said to hold "in every Region" (the West and Northeast are exceptions the Results section itself notes), and D districts said to get more federal revenue than A to C districts (C districts get more). See audit items 8–10.
- [checkable] The Figure 4 prose (p17–18) quotes gap values that cannot be read off the printed Figure 4. The D–A % Black gap is given as 13.4 pp in 1988–89 (the plot shows about 10 pp, with no shrinkage by 2018–19). The A–D % White gap is given as "around 35 percentage points" (plot about 27–29 pp; p16 Table 4 A = 0.30). The Simpson's gaps are said to have "surpassed −0.08" (plot about 0.05–0.06). See audit item 11.
- [checkable] Table 1 (p9) lists 5,124 schools for the student-performance sample, but every N in Table 5 (p19) is larger or different: 6,890, 5,193 and 6,183. Nothing explains the gap. The Table 5 Ns may count a different unit, but the reader is not told.
- [checkable] The paper contradicts itself on test-score change. p19 concludes that D-neighborhood schools "are not improving quickly enough to close the gap," based on the cohort-trend outcome in Table 5. Then p21 says the performance findings "do not reveal whether the gaps have changed over time."
- [judgment] Causal and mechanism language drifts well past the stated correlational design. The abstract says "the consequences of redlining persist" and the historic policies "continue to shape educational outcomes today." The introduction (p3) says D districts receive more Title I "because their schools educate more low-income students," although Title I is never measured separately (only total federal revenue). p3 invokes "two mediating channels," which the paper never tests. p12 says the local gap "mediates" federal/state funds. Policy Implications (p22) speaks of "redlining's impacts on property values," though no exhibit measures property values.
- [judgment] The abstract leaves out the finding that cuts most against its funding story: schools in D neighborhoods have the highest per-pupil total expenditures (p15 Table 3, all Overall A/B/C coefficients negative). It also says these schools "predominantly educate Black ... students," while the D-neighborhood mean is 36% Black nationally and 9% in the West (p16 Table 4 constants). The abstract never names the design (descriptive regressions with CBSA fixed effects and no controls).
- [judgment] Across all four tables the region-by-region prose mostly just recites table cells, and it does this selectively. It lists some non-significant cells and silently skips others (for example, p11 names federal D–C as non-significant in the Northeast and South but not in the West, \$182 (\$151), and omits South D–B, −\$349 (\$313)). The reader ends up doing the table-reading anyway.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Tables 2–5 directly rather than the region-by-region prose. The sign convention is "grade X minus D" (D is the reference), so in Table 2 a positive PPR coefficient means A/B/C districts have more than D, while in Table 3 negative PPE coefficients mean A/B/C schools spend less than D schools. The prose switches between signed and unsigned values (for example, p11 gives the state D–A gap as "\$3670" while Table 2 shows −\$3670).
- The stars in every table use *p < .10. When the prose calls a difference "statistically significant," it often means p < .10 (for example, the national D–A total PPR of \$1546, SE \$822, p12 Table 2).
- Do not use Figure 3 (p13) for anything. The finance trend claims on p13–14 and the "persistent and growing" statement on p20 cannot be checked without Supplemental Table A4(A).
- Before quoting any over-time number for racial diversity (p17–18), check it against Figure 4 yourself. Several quoted gaps do not match the plotted values. The prose numbers may come from Supplemental Table A4(B), which was not available for this review.
- The most important single result for interpretation is the reversal between Table 2 and Table 3: D districts have less revenue, yet D-neighborhood schools spend the most. Read p14–15 ("Comparing the District and School Finance Results") carefully. Its FRPL numbers (79.3%, −0.37, −0.06) and the within-district allocation argument rest entirely on Supplemental Table A8 and Figures A6, A7 and A10, which are not in the article.
- For performance, the robust finding is the level gap (Table 5, first panel). Learning-rate coefficients are mostly non-significant, while test-score-change coefficients are significant nationally but tiny (0.004–0.010 SD). Ignore the "virtually no statistically significant differences" sentence on p18. The "1.9 grade levels" conversion (p18) comes with no stated SD-per-grade factor.
- A district's "grade" is an area-weighted average over only the HOLC-graded portion of the district, discretized at 1.5/2.5/3.5 (p10). The paper does not report how much of each district is graded, so "D district" means "mostly D among its graded area," not "mostly redlined."
- Skimmable: the literature review (p3–7) is standard background. The robustness paragraphs (p12–13, p19–20) and Policy Implications (p22–23) summarize supplemental material and are not independent evidence.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization and navigability.* The three-outcome structure works. Each block opens by naming its table, gives the national result, then walks through the regions. The cost is length and repetition. The finance section alone (p11–15) recites more than 30 table cells, and it chooses which cells to mention inconsistently, so a reader who trusts the prose to flag exceptions will miss some. The Methods section is compact but muddled in one place. p10 says the model quantifies how D units differ "from the set of all other HOLC schools or districts (e.g., A, B, C)," which describes a pooled D-versus-rest contrast. The model and tables instead estimate three separate A, B and C coefficients against D. The same paragraph calls HOLC_A, HOLC_B and HOLC_C "the estimated average differences." They are the indicators; the β coefficients are the differences. Endnote 1 (p23, a terminology note on "D districts") is attached on p10 to a sentence about bin cutoffs. Figure captions are inconsistent: Figure 3 describes regressions on "A to D indicators," Figure 4 on "A to C indicators." Both captions mention cluster-robust standard errors, but neither figure shows any interval. The Table 4 note says "All dollars denominated in USD 2018" for a table containing no dollars.

*Fidelity of argument.* The cross-sectional story (lower local revenue and lower total revenue for D districts, more Black and fewer White students, lower test scores) is faithfully reported at the national level. The problems start where the paper interprets and generalizes. (1) "Progressive" federal money is described as favoring D over A to C districts (p12, p20), but C districts receive significantly more federal revenue than D districts nationally (\$253***, p12 Table 2) and in the Midwest (\$361***). (2) The longitudinal finance claims cannot be checked at all because of the Figure 3 error, yet the Discussion treats them as established. (3) The Figure 4 narrative contradicts itself. On p18 the D–A and D–B Simpson's gaps "continued to grow through 2018–2019." A few lines later D schools are "converging toward the already-rising trajectories" of A–C schools, and the paragraph ends "gaps ... persisted and often widened," while the % Black paragraph just above says those gaps shrank. Reading the plot, D–A Simpson's gaps are roughly flat from 2008–09 (about 0.05) to 2018–19 (about 0.056), and C schools are not "flat" as p18 says (about 0.37 to about 0.46). (4) The performance paragraph on p18 calls the trend differences both "small as a share of the total variation" and "a large share of the between-school standard deviation," so the reader gets no clear verdict.

*Abstract and front-end summary.* The abstract accurately gives the scope (144 CBSAs, p9 Table 1) and the direction of the district-finance, demographic and test-score findings. It overstates in three ways: its causal framing ("consequences," "continue to shape"), "predominantly educate Black" students, and the silent omission of the school-level spending reversal. The p3 summary repeats the Title I "because" claim and adds untested "mediating channels." A reader who stops at the abstract would not learn that the design is a set of descriptive fixed-effects regressions with no controls, or that schools in D neighborhoods are the best-funded schools in the sample.

*Causal framing.* The design statement (p9–10) and the p21 disclaimer are clear, but they sit between a causal abstract and introduction and a Policy Implications section that speaks of "redlining's impacts on property values" and "redlining's impact on neighborhood demographic stratification" (p22). The "first to document" priority claim (p22) and "the ability to predict ... is compelling" (p22) are rhetorical, not results. The policy recommendation that "additional resources ... may be necessary to support students in D-graded neighborhoods" (p22) does not engage with Table 3's finding that these schools already spend the most per pupil.

*What cannot be checked.* Everything attributed only to the supplement: the FRPL results (p14–15, Supplemental Table A8), the within-district allocation claims (Figures A6, A7, A10), the binned-scatter robustness (Figure A5), panel-versus-full-sample comparisons (Table A5), the with/without FE comparison (Table A6), covariate models (Table A7), the between-school SDs of 0.07 and 0.04 used on p18, and the true coefficient series behind Figures 3 and 4 (Tables A4(A) and A4(B)). I have not speculated about these values.

##### Text-versus-table audit

All items below were confirmed on the rendered PDF pages (Table 2 p12, Table 3 p15, Table 4 p16, Table 5 p19, Table 1 p9, Figures 3 p13 and 4 p17; prose on p10, p11, p14, p16–21). Figure values are read from the plotted markers (pixel-measured against the gridlines, accuracy about ±0.005).

1. **p11 prose vs p12 Table 2, PPR total, West column, B row.** Prose says: "Nationwide and across all four Regions, total PPRs are lower for districts with a higher proportion of D neighborhoods." Table says: West B = −\$1082*** (\$307), so B districts have *less* total revenue than D districts in the West. The prose itself concedes this later in the same paragraph.
2. **p12 prose vs p12 Table 2, PPR federal, Overall and Midwest columns, C row.** Prose says the federal and state funds "favor D districts relative to A to C districts." Table says: C = +\$253*** (\$76) Overall and +\$361*** (\$101) Midwest, so C districts receive more federal revenue than D. (The p11 prose reports the \$253 correctly; the p12 synthesis and p20 Discussion ignore it.)
3. **p14 prose vs p15 Table 3, PPE total, Midwest column, A and B rows.** Prose says: schools in A and B neighborhoods "have statistically significant higher spending (\$302 and \$202, respectively)." Table says: \$302 (\$555) and \$202 (\$630), with no stars, so neither is significant.
4. **p14 prose vs p15 Table 3, PPE federal, Overall column, C row.** Prose says: "the smallest between A and C (\$141, SE = \$31)." Table says: C row = −\$141*** (\$31). This is the D–C comparison (C relative to D), and the sign is negative. The label is wrong and the sign is dropped.
5. **p18 prose vs p19 Table 5, Avg. student math and ELA scores, Northeast column, Constant row.** Prose says: "highest average scores in the Northeast (−0.023 SD, SE = 0.02)." Table says: −0.225*** (0.021).
6. **p18 prose vs p19 Table 5, Avg. student test score change, Overall column, A/B/C rows.** Prose says: "Nationwide, there are virtually no statistically significant differences across HOLC grades for average student learning rates and average student test score trends." Table says: test score change A = 0.01*** (0.003), B = 0.007*** (0.002), C = 0.004*** (0.001), all significant at p < .01. Learning-rate B and C are also significant at p < .10. The same p18 paragraph later quotes these three coefficients.
7. **p9 Table 1 vs p19 Table 5, Student performance, Schools.** Table 1 says: 5,124 schools. Table 5 Ns: 6,890 (scores), 5,193 (learning), 6,183 (test score change). No N matches, and the largest exceeds the Table 1 count.
8. **p20 Discussion vs p15 Table 3, PPE state and local, Overall column, B and C rows.** Prose says: "The differences in per-pupil state/local expenditures between schools in D and A, B, and C neighborhoods are insignificant." Table says: B = −\$1010* (\$590), C = −\$745** (\$323). Only A (−\$1131, \$860) is insignificant. The p14 Results text says this correctly.
9. **p21 Discussion vs p16 Table 4, % Black West column and Simpson's Northeast column.** Prose says: "in every Region schools in D neighborhoods have higher shares of Black and non-White students and less diverse student bodies." Table says: West % Black A/B/C = −0.01, −0.02, −0.01, none significant. Northeast Simpson's A/B/C = 0.04, 0.02, 0.01, none significant. The p16–17 Results text itself names both exceptions.
10. **p20 Discussion vs p12 Table 2, PPR federal, Overall column, C row.** Prose says: "districts with D neighborhoods receive higher per-pupil federal and state revenues than districts with A to C neighborhoods." Table says: federal C = +\$253*** (C above D). State C = −\$461 (\$495) is not significant.
11. **p17–18 prose vs p17 Figure 4.** (a) Panel A, % Black, D–A gap: prose says 13.4 pp in 1988–89, shrinking to 10.3 pp by 2018–19. The plot shows D ≈ 0.346 and A ≈ 0.248 in 1988–89 (about 9.8 pp), and D ≈ 0.302 and A ≈ 0.199 in 2018–19 (about 10.3 pp), so the gap does not shrink. (b) Panel A, A and B peaks in 1998–99: prose says "24.8% and 26.5%." The plot shows A ≈ 0.257 and B ≈ 0.247; 24.8% is A's 1988–89 value. (c) Panel A, D–B and D–C gaps: prose says they begin at 10.8 and 7.8 pp and end at 7.4 and 6.5 pp. The plot shows about 10.5 and 5.7 pp in 1988–89 and about 9.5 and 5.8 pp in 2018–19. (d) Panel B, % White, A–D gap: prose says "around 35 percentage points." The plot shows about 26.6 pp in 1988–89 and about 28.6 pp in 2018–19 (p16 Table 4 cross-section: A = 0.30). (e) Panel C, Simpson's D–A and D–B gaps: prose says they "surpassed −0.08 in 2018–2019." The plot shows A ≈ 0.487, B ≈ 0.481, D ≈ 0.431, gaps of about 0.056 and 0.050. (f) Panel C: prose says the index was "remaining flat" for C and D schools. The plot shows C rising from ≈ 0.371 to ≈ 0.459. If the quoted numbers come from Supplemental Table A4(B) with a specification different from the plotted one, the paper does not say so.
12. **p13–14 prose vs p13 Figure 3.** Panels A, B and D plot the same values as Figure 4 Panels A, B and C. They have the same y-axis ranges (0.20–0.35, 0.20–0.60, 0.35–0.50), and marker positions measured on both figures agree to within 0.001 (for example, 1998–99 in Figure 3 Panel A: 0.346/0.288/0.257/0.248, the same as the % Black series in Figure 4 Panel A). The figure therefore cannot show the dollar revenue its caption promises. Specific prose-versus-panel conflicts: total revenue gap "favors A to C districts" vs Panel A with D highest at every point. Local revenue "more significant initial funding gaps in the late 1980s" vs Panel D with all grades between about 0.35 and 0.37 in 1988–89. Federal revenue favoring "C, D" vs Panel B with D lowest at every point. "Large positive spike ... for 2009–2010" vs no 2009–10 data point.
13. **p13 Figure 3 caption and x-axis vs p7 Data section and p9 Table 1.** The caption says "1989 to 2018," and Table 1 gives the finance time series as 1989–2018. The F-33 data are said to run 1989–1990 to 2017–2018 (p7), yet the axis is labeled 1988–1989 through 2018–2019.
14. **p13 and p17 figure captions.** Figure 3 says the averages come from a regression "on A to D indicators," while Figure 4 says "on A to C indicators" (the Methods use D as the omitted category). Both captions report "cluster-robust standard errors," but neither figure displays any.
15. **p8 Figure 2 legend vs p8 Figure 2 note.** The map legend reads "HOLC Map CBSA (141)". The note says "There are 144 present-day CBSAs" (30+54+45+15 = 144), which matches the abstract and p9 Table 1 finance column. The 141 in the legend matches Table 1's racial-diversity column instead.

Checked and consistent (no mismatch): the p11 total, federal, state and local PPR constants, D–A/D–B/D–C magnitudes, percentages (10%, 7%) and regional significance statements other than item 1. The p14 PPE total constant, the A and C gaps and their percentages (9%, 5%), and the state/local A/B/C values. The p16 national % Black and Simpson's values, the regional D-group constants (South 0.48, West 0.09, Midwest White 0.18, West White 0.11), and the West and Northeast exceptions. The p18 national D constant (−0.37), D–A gap (0.64, SE 0.04), West constant (−0.461), Northeast learning-rate A (0.02, SE 0.01), and the 25%/18%/10% ratios given the stated SD of 0.04. The p13 and p17 sample reductions (1760 to 1109; 9709 to 4677) against p9 Table 1.
