### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper links 1935–40 HOLC neighborhood grades to present-day districts and schools across 144 metros. It gives the field its first broad, public-data description of how those grades line up with today's district revenue, school spending, school racial composition, and test scores. The best-supported findings are within-metro cross-sectional gaps: a large local-revenue gap for mostly-D districts, and large differences in racial composition and average scores for schools inside D polygons. Those findings are useful and credible as description. The historical-causal framing the paper builds on them is not credible at the same strength. The 30-year finance time series, one of the pieces advertised as new, is not supported by the figure printed in the article.

**Strengths:**

- **A new, reusable linkage.** The paper overlays the digitized HOLC polygons on 2018–19 district boundaries and school points across 144 CBSAs (p.8; p.9, Table 1: 1,760 districts for finance, 9,709 schools for diversity, 5,124 schools for achievement). All inputs are public (Mapping Inequality, F-33, NERD\$, NCES, SEDA). This scale and the school-level (not just tract-level) outcomes are new relative to the HOLC literature the paper reviews (pp.2–7). Others can easily extend it.
- **A three-outcome portrait within metros.** CBSA fixed effects mean every comparison is within a metro. Nationally, schools in D polygons are 36% Black and 14% White (p.16, Table 4, Overall constants 0.36 (SE 0.011) and 0.14 (SE 0.007)). Schools in A polygons are 14 points less Black and 30 points more White (A rows: −0.14 (0.027), 0.30 (0.022)). Their average scores are 0.643 SD higher (p.19, Table 5, avg. scores, Overall, A row: 0.643 (SE 0.04)), and the gradient is monotone across A to D. The score gradient holds in all four regions (A rows 0.541–0.753).
- **An informative contrast between district revenue and school spending.** This is the paper's most useful substantive result, and it is under-sold. Mostly-D districts raise far less local revenue: D constant \$5,240 against an A–D gap of \$5,937 (SE \$1,228), so A districts raise roughly twice as much locally (p.12, Table 2, PPR local, Overall). State and federal aid offset most of that gap: A–D state −\$3,670 (SE \$752), federal −\$722 (SE \$139). The remaining total gap is \$1,546 (SE \$822). The components add up exactly (5,937 − 3,670 − 722 ≈ 1,546). Yet schools located in D polygons spend more per pupil than schools in A polygons (p.15, Table 3, PPE total, Overall, A row: −\$1,539 (SE \$852); federal −\$602 (SE \$39)). A single paper that shows both the local-revenue deficit and the offsetting within-district and intergovernmental redistribution is valuable for school-finance readers.
- **Regional heterogeneity that corrects a national, Black-centered narrative.** In the West, schools in D polygons are 9% Black and A–D Black-share gaps are near zero (p.16, Table 4, West: constant 0.09; A −0.01 (0.03)). The West also shows no A–D total-revenue gap (p.12, Table 2, West, PPR total, A: \$29 (SE \$647)). So the pattern is not uniform, and the paper reports that honestly in its tables.
- **Its stated method is appropriately modest.** The Methods section calls the design "a more conservative correlational approach" (pp.9–10). The Discussion states that "this article's results are not causal" (p.21). The research questions (p.2) are framed as comparisons.

**Weaknesses:**

- **[checkable] Figure 3, the 1989–2018 district finance time series, cannot be the finance series its caption describes.** Its y-axes run from 0.20 to 0.80 (p.13, Figure 3, all panels). Those are proportions, not per-pupil dollars (the caption says "USD 2018"). Panels A, B and D match panels A, B and C of the diversity figure (p.17, Figure 4: % Black, % White, Simpson's index). I checked this on the rendered pages and by pixel comparison of the embedded images: after a 9-pixel vertical offset, the top panels have a mean absolute difference of about 2 on a 0–255 scale. So the article's evidence for the claim that district finance gaps are "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018" (p.20) is not displayed anywhere in the published text. The coefficients reportedly sit in Supplemental Table A4(A) (note 3), which I could not access. The longitudinal finance result should not be cited from this article as printed.
- **[judgment] The paper's framing and its design disagree.** The Methods section is correlational (pp.9–10), and p.21 says "not causal." The abstract, however, says "the consequences of redlining persist today" and "the historic policies that shaped neighborhoods continue to shape educational outcomes today" (p.1). The Discussion calls the predictive power "compelling" and infers "an entrenched connection rooted in past policies" (p.22). The policy section speaks of "redlining's impacts on property values" (p.22). The design cannot tell three things apart: (i) any effect of the HOLC maps themselves; (ii) the 1930s neighborhood status the grades recorded; and (iii) everything that has happened to these places since. The paper's own reference list includes Fishback et al. (2020), whose title says the maps reflected how "race and poverty influenced" the grading. It also includes Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder (2021), which uses boundary designs because raw grade comparisons are confounded. My recollection, not re-verified here, is that the latter finds real but partially fading map effects.
- **[judgment] It is unclear how much the HOLC label adds beyond "these neighborhoods are poor and non-White today."** That D-graded areas are poorer and less White today is established in work the paper cites (pp.4–5). That such schools score lower is the familiar SES–achievement gradient (p.5, citing Reardon 2016). The paper's own FRPL regression shows a 37-point A–D gap in low-income share (pp.14–15: D 79.3%, A −0.37 (SE 0.02); table in the unavailable Supplemental A8). A 0.64 SD score gap is roughly what that composition gap would predict. The paper never asks whether HOLC grade predicts outcomes after conditioning on current neighborhood or student SES. The one conditioning exercise (Supplemental Table A7, p.20) uses covariates from Markley (2021), apparently 1930s area-description fields, on a smaller sample. It is reported in one sentence and cannot be inspected. That exercise speaks to whether the grade carries information beyond 1930s conditions, which is arguably the most interesting test for a legacy paper. It is buried.
- **[checkable] Mechanisms are asserted, not measured.** The Data section (pp.7–8) uses no property-value, assessed-value, or tax-base data. The local-revenue gap is attributed to property values by citation alone (pp.11, 20–21). "Redlining's impacts on property values are associated with the inability of districts... to raise local property tax revenues" (p.22) is therefore not something this paper shows.
- **[checkable] The headline total-revenue gap is fragile, but the text states it more firmly.** Nationally, the A–D total gap is significant only at p<.1 (\$1,546, SE \$822), and it is not significant in any region (p.12, Table 2, PPR total, A row: Midwest \$1,891 (\$1,306), NE \$2,343 (\$1,490), South \$1,973 (\$2,484), West \$29 (\$647)). The text on p.11 says total revenue is lower for D districts "Nationwide and across all four Regions." In the West, however, B districts have \$1,082 less total revenue than D districts (SE \$307). The robust finance result is the local-revenue gap, which is significant for A–D in every region (Table 2, PPR local, A row).
- **[checkable] Several text-versus-table errors, confirmed on the rendered pages, affect numbers readers are likely to quote.**
  - The average D-school score in the Northeast is given as "−0.023 SD" in the text (p.18), but Table 5 shows −0.225 (SE 0.021) (p.19, Table 5, Northeast constant).
  - The text calls the Midwest A and B total-spending differences "statistically significant (\$302 and \$202)" (p.14). Table 3 gives \$302 (\$555) and \$202 (\$630) with no stars (p.15).
  - The Discussion says school state/local spending differences are "insignificant" (p.20). The results text (p.14) and Table 3 show B −\$1,010* (\$590) and C −\$745** (\$323).
  - The text reports "virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends (p.18). Table 5 shows all three national trend contrasts significant at p<.01 (A 0.01 (0.003), B 0.007 (0.002), C 0.004 (0.001)).
  - The achievement regressions report N = 6,890 (p.19, Table 5), but Table 1 lists 5,124 schools for that sample (p.9).
  - The introduction says D districts "receive more federal Title I funding" (p.3). The paper observes only total federal revenue, and C districts receive more of it than D districts (p.12, Table 2, PPR federal, C: +\$253 (SE \$76)).
- **[checkable] The abstract's demographic claim overreaches.** The abstract says schools in these areas "predominantly educate Black... students" (p.1). D-polygon schools are 36% Black nationally and 9% Black in the West (p.16, Table 4, % Black constants). "Predominantly non-White and low-income" is supported (White 14%; FRPL 79.3%, p.14). "Predominantly Black" is not.
- **[judgment] The diversity time series undercuts the "legacy" reading for that outcome.** The text says Simpson's-index gaps between grades were "near zero" in 1988–89 and opened afterward (p.18). As far as the plot can be read, it agrees (p.17, Figure 4C). A gap that appears in the 1990s–2010s is more naturally attributed to recent demographic change and resorting than to a 1930s map. The same paragraph is internally inconsistent: the gap "continued to grow" versus the D series "converging" in the last decade. Read from the plot, the 2018–19 A–D gap looks closer to 0.05–0.06 than the "surpassed −0.08" in the text; that reading is approximate. The Black-share gap narrows over the period, from 13.4 to 10.3 points (p.17). The "persistence despite desegregation and SFR" argument (pp.3, 22) also has no counterfactual, and the series begins in 1989.
- **[judgment] The novelty claim is partly dated.** "This article is the first to document the relationship between HOLC grades and modern educational outcomes" (p.22). This is in tension with the paper's own citation of Aaronson et al. (2023), which found effects on children's educational attainment (p.5), unless "educational outcomes" means school-system outcomes. I also verified by web search that the same findings have circulated since November 2021 as EdWorkingPaper 21-363 (Lukes & Cleveland), with media and policy coverage. The 2026 article therefore mostly formalizes a result the field already has, not a new finding. The search also surfaced a single-city study of Oakland school segregation and grey-literature analyses of Michigan district finance. I did not verify their content or dates.
- **[judgment] The policy implications do not follow from the evidence.** The paper proposes restructuring local property-tax reliance, METCO-style transfers, MTO-style housing moves, and using HOLC maps to prioritize interventions (pp.22–23). None is tested. Targeting by HOLC grade is not shown to improve on current measures that already exist (FRPL, SEDA, tract income).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for** the within-metro descriptive fact that schools located in 1930s D-graded polygons today enroll far more non-White and low-income students and post much lower average scores than schools in A-graded polygons. National A–D score gap: 0.643 SD (SE 0.04) (p.19, Table 5). Share Black: 0.36 in D against 0.22 in A (p.16, Table 4). Share White: 0.14 against 0.44. The gradient is monotone across grades and the score gap appears in every region.
- **Cite it for** the district local-revenue gap and its partial offset. A–D local revenue per pupil: \$5,937 (SE \$1,228), about double the D level. State offset: \$3,670 (SE \$752). Federal: \$722 (SE \$139). The net total gap is about \$1,546 and only marginally significant (p.12, Table 2, Overall). Quote the local gap as the robust number. Quote the total gap only with its caveat.
- **Cite it for** the finding that nominal per-pupil spending at the school level runs the other way: D-polygon schools spend about \$1,539 more than A-polygon schools (p<.1) and \$602 more in federal funds (p.15, Table 3). The shortfall sits in district revenue, not in nominal school spending. Need-adjusted comparisons are not made.
- **Do not cite it for** "schools in redlined neighborhoods are underfunded." At the school level the paper finds the opposite in nominal terms (Table 3). The title's word "Funding" invites this misreading.
- **Do not cite it for** a causal effect of redlining or of the HOLC maps on school outcomes. The design is a difference in means with CBSA fixed effects and no controls (p.10; p.12, Table 2 note), and the authors disclaim causality (pp.9–10, 21) even though the abstract does not.
- **Do not cite it for** district finance gaps "growing" from 1989 to 2018. The printed Figure 3 (p.13) shows proportion-scale series that duplicate the diversity figure, and the supporting table is only in the supplement.
- **Do not cite it for** property values as the mechanism. The paper measures none, and that link rests on other studies.
- **Do not cite it for** "predominantly Black" schools nationally. The figure is 36% overall and 9% in the West (Table 4). Do not cite the Northeast D-school mean as −0.023 SD; Table 5 gives −0.225.
- **Scope when generalizing.** The sample covers HOLC-mapped metros only (p.8 says it includes all CBSAs with at least one HOLC grade). The "15% of major U.S. metropolitan areas" figure on p.3 has an unclear denominator. Schools outside polygons are dropped (p.10), so the school results describe the old urban cores that existed by the late 1930s, not the metros. A district enters the sample with any polygon overlap and is graded on the HOLC-covered part of its area only (p.10). A "D district" may therefore be a large district whose mapped portion is a small old core. All estimates are enrollment-weighted, so large urban districts dominate. The South and West district samples are thin (Table 2, N = 187 and 159). Sample composition is described only in unavailable supplements (A1–A3).
- **Open questions the paper sets up but does not answer.**
  - Does grade predict outcomes conditional on current neighborhood SES, and conditional on 1930s conditions? (Only the unavailable Table A7 addresses the latter.)
  - How much of the local-revenue gap runs through assessed property values versus composition, commercial tax base, or district fragmentation?
  - Is the achievement gap larger than composition alone would predict, and what are need-adjusted spending comparisons?
  - How do gentrifying D areas behave? (Figure 4's rising diversity for A and B schools hints at resorting.)
  - What do boundary designs, of the kind Aaronson and coauthors use, show when applied to school attendance zones and district lines?
  - What is the corrected finance time series?

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What is genuinely new.* The contribution is infrastructural and descriptive. The paper takes the digitized HOLC maps, which have already been joined to house prices, mobility, health, heat and crime, and joins them for the first time at scale to the three things school-policy readers care about: district revenue, school composition, and school achievement. It does so across essentially all mapped metros, with within-metro comparisons. The pieces that are new to the literature are, in order of value:

1. The contrast between district revenue and school spending (Tables 2 and 3). A mostly-D district raises about half the local revenue per pupil of a mostly-A district. Intergovernmental aid closes roughly three quarters of that gap. Within-district allocation then leaves schools in D polygons with somewhat higher nominal per-pupil spending than schools in A polygons.
2. The school-level achievement gradient (Table 5).
3. The linkage method itself.

The 30-year series would have been a fourth new piece. For finance, the figure printed in the article is evidently the wrong one: its axes are on a 0–1 scale, and three of its four panels reproduce Figure 4. For diversity, the series shows gaps that emerge rather than persist.

*What is repackaged.* The demographic and achievement findings are close to what one would predict by combining two literatures the paper itself cites. First, D-graded areas remain poorer and less White (pp.4–5). Second, poorer, less-White schools score lower (p.5). The paper's contribution there is quantification in a common frame, not surprise. The deeper problem for a paper titled "Lingering Legacy" is that it never asks what the HOLC grade adds. If the grade matters only through today's neighborhood composition, then "redlining's legacy" in schools is simply "neighborhood poverty in schools," restated with a historical label. That may be true and important, but this design cannot establish the historical attribution. The authors' own summary of Supplemental Table A7 (p.20) suggests the grade predicts outcomes beyond 1930s area characteristics. If that holds, it is the most legacy-relevant result in the project, and it deserves main-text treatment. As published, readers cannot evaluate it.

*Most quotable versus best-supported claim.* The most quotable claims are the abstract's "the historic policies that shaped neighborhoods continue to shape educational outcomes today" and p.22's "the ability to predict current educational outcomes... based on grades from 1935 to 1940 is compelling." Both carry causal and historical weight that the correlational design (the authors' own word, pp.9–10) cannot support. The best-supported claim is narrower and still useful. Within the same metro today, schools located inside 1930s D-graded polygons serve student bodies that are about 86% non-White and about 79% FRPL-eligible, and they score about two-thirds of a standard deviation below schools inside A-graded polygons. Districts covering mostly D-graded areas raise about half as much local revenue per pupil, and state and federal aid close most of that gap. Anyone citing the paper should cite the second version.

*Standing in the literature and generalizability.* Aaronson and coauthors use boundary and comparison-city designs to identify effects of the maps on neighborhoods and children, including educational attainment. The present paper is descriptive and should not be cited as evidence on its own that the maps caused anything in schools. It is the best available broad descriptive benchmark for HOLC grade × school outcomes. Its descriptive claims are bounded to the old urban cores of mapped metros, weighted toward large districts, and weaker in the South and West, where district samples are small. The paper states some of this (the regional tables are candid) but never says it plainly in the abstract or conclusion. The descriptive benchmark has been public since the 2021 working paper, so the published version's added value lies mainly in its expanded robustness material, much of which sits in a supplement unavailable to this review. The printed errors also reduce how far readers can rely on the article's text, as opposed to its tables. The confirmed errors are the Figure 3 duplication, the Northeast −0.023 versus −0.225 slip, the significance statements that contradict Tables 3 and 5, and the sample-size mismatch between Tables 1 and 5.

*Bottom line.* This is a modest, useful descriptive contribution on a question of real public interest. Its credible core is the within-metro cross-section, and the Table 2 local-revenue and Table 5 average-score results in particular are quotable with confidence. It is oversold in its framing and policy sections, and one of its advertised novel components, the finance time series, is not supported by the article as printed. That combination is why I rate it Adequate rather than Strong. The core facts are clear and well-measured enough that I do not rate it Weak.

*Verified versus recalled.* I verified by web search the existence and November 2021 date of EdWorkingPaper 21-363 by the same authors with the same title and findings. I verified from the paper's reference list the titles and venues of Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder (2021, AEJ: Economic Policy), Aaronson et al. (2023, JEL), and Fishback et al. (2020, NBER w28146). My characterization of the Aaronson et al. and Fishback et al. findings comes from recall. The Oakland and Michigan studies turned up in search results only, and I did not examine them.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

Every input to this study is public, and the headline cross-sectional tables (Tables 2–5) report everything a regression table should: coefficients, clustered SEs, R², F, N, the fixed effects, and the weights. But the paper has no data or code availability statement, names no software, and gives no replication package. Its description of the GIS linkage leaves out steps that the authors' own 2021 working paper documented and that change the sample (NYC sub-districts, charter/point-located districts, "E"-graded polygons). And the published Figure 3, which is supposed to show district per-pupil revenue over time, actually reprints the racial-diversity series from Figure 4. So the paper's claims about finance over time cannot be checked from the article, and several sample counts and text-vs-table numbers do not reconcile.

**Strengths:**

- All six data sources are public and cited with URLs or retrieval dates (p.24–28 references: Nelson et al. 2020 Mapping Inequality, retrieved Oct 20, 2020; Edunomics Lab 2021 NERD\$ "version 1"; Reardon et al. 2021 SEDA 4.0, retrieved Feb 8, 2021; Markley 2021; U.S. Census Bureau 2020 TIGER/Line; NCES ELSi). No restricted-use data are involved.
- The district grade is stated as an explicit formula: an area-weighted mean of grade codes 1–4 over polygon–district intersection areas (p.10, rendered equation). The cutpoints are also explicit: 1–1.5 = A, 1.5–2.5 = B, 2.5–3.5 = C, 3.5–4 = D (p.10). The main specification is written out: the outcome on A/B/C indicators (D is the reference) plus CBSA fixed effects (p.10).
- Every table note states the weighting and the SE clustering (CBSA-clustered), and says no controls are included (p.12 Table 2; p.15 Table 3; p.16 Table 4; p.19 Table 5).
- Every cross-sectional model reports its SE, R², F, and N, broken out nationally and by Region (Table 2 p.12; Table 3 p.15; Table 4 p.16; Table 5 p.19). The regional Ns sum to the overall N in every panel I checked: Table 2 806+608+187+159 = 1,760; Table 3 2,744+3,466+1,340+1,473 = 9,023; Table 4 3,031+3,595+1,453+1,630 = 9,709; Table 5 2,181+2,576+1,042+1,091 = 6,890.
- Table 1 (p.9) gives sample sizes for each outcome group (schools, districts, CBSAs, and cross-dataset matches). Figure 2 (p.8) gives the CBSA counts by Region (30/54/45/15 = 144).
- The sensitivity checks the paper describes are the right ones for this design: a non-discretized weighted average, a schools'-average grade, with and without CBSA FE, a covariate-adjusted model, and full-sample vs. panel-sample comparisons (p.12–13, p.19–20). All of them are in the supplement, though (see below).

**Weaknesses:**

- [checkable] The paper has no data availability statement, no code availability statement, and no replication package. The back matter on p.23 has Acknowledgments, ORCIDs, Funding, Conflicts, a one-line "Supplemental material for this article is available online," and Notes, with nothing about data or code. I found no deposited code on the EdWorkingPapers page for the 2021 version (ai21-363), on OSF, or on GitHub. The journal's supplement page returned HTTP 403, so I could not check it.
- [checkable] The paper names no software for the GIS overlay, the area calculations, the regressions, or the binscatter. The binscatter citation (Cattaneo et al., 2024; p.12) and the Stata-style wording ("margins plots," endnotes 2, 4, 5, 7, p.23; "analytic weight," Figure 3 caption p.13) suggest Stata, and the 2021 working paper (fn. 9) says ArcGIS "completely contains" was used for the point-in-polygon join. The published article states neither.
- [checkable] Published Figure 3 (p.13, "District per-pupil revenue by HOLC grade") does not show revenue. On the rendered page, panels A (total), B (federal), and D (local) have the same plotted points, axis scales, and line patterns as Figure 4's panels A (% Black), B (% White), and C (Simpson's index) on p.17. Only the titles differ. The y-axes run 0.20–0.35, 0.20–0.60, 0.40–0.80, and 0.35–0.50, which cannot be 2018 dollars given Table 2's constants of \$14,402 total and \$1,201 federal (p.12). Panel B puts A districts highest in federal revenue, the reverse of Table 2 (A = −\$722, p.12). The text's "spike in per-pupil federal funding … for 2009–2010" (p.14) has no matching point on the x-axis, whose points are 1988–89, 1998–99, 2008–09, and 2018–19. The 2021 working paper's version of this figure (its Figure 4, p.60) is in dollars with points at 1989–90, 1999–00, 2009–10, and 2017–18. The coefficients behind the published figure exist only in Supplemental Table A4(A) (endnote 3, p.23), which I could not access.
- [checkable] Table 1 lists 5,124 schools in the student-performance sample (p.9), but the Ns in Table 5 are all larger: 6,890 for average scores, 5,193 for learning rates, and 6,183 for score trends (p.19). The paper does not explain the gap. The 2021 working paper has the same gap (5,124 in its text; N = 6,890 in its Table 7).
- [checkable] Some numbers in the text do not match the tables (both confirmed on the rendered pages):
  - Northeast D-school average score: the text says −0.023 SD (p.18); Table 5 says −0.225 (SE 0.021) (p.19).
  - Midwest school spending: the text calls the A and B spending gaps "statistically significant (\$302 and \$202)" (p.14), but Table 3 shows \$302 (SE \$555) and \$202 (SE \$630) with no stars (p.15).
- [checkable] Several Figure 4 values quoted in the text do not match what the figure shows. My readings from the rendered p.17 are approximate (within about 0.005):
  - The D–A gap in % Black in 1988–89 is given as 13.4 pp in the text (p.17); the figure shows about 9.7 pp.
  - The text says A and B schools reached 24.8% and 26.5% Black in 1998–99. The figure shows about 25.7% for A and 24.7% for B, i.e., reversed.
  - The text puts the A–D gap in % White at "around 35 percentage points" (p.18); the figure shows about 27–29 pp.
  - The text says the Simpson's-index gaps "surpassed −0.08" by 2018–19 (p.18); the figure shows about 0.05.

  The text may be quoting FE-adjusted coefficients from the unavailable Supplemental Table A4(B) rather than the plotted means, but the paper does not say which.
- [checkable] The published article omits pipeline steps that the authors' November 2021 EdWorkingPaper documents and that change the sample:
  - NYC's 32 community school districts were substituted using NYC Department of City Planning boundaries (WP fn. 3).
  - Districts without polygons, such as charter LEAs, were assigned by point location (WP p.20, fn. 13).
  - Schools in "E"-graded polygons were dropped (WP fn. 10).
  - SEDA OLS estimates were chosen over EB (WP fn. 7).
  - Simpson's index uses seven race categories (WP fn. 6).

  On p.7–8 the article says only that SEDA estimates "are calculated using ordinary least squares (OLS) and Empirical Bayes" and never states the number of race categories.
- [checkable] The published article and the working paper describe the per-pupil school finance measures differently. The article says "we transform all financial data into per-pupil terms using the district or school's total enrollment" (p.7). The WP says NERD\$ per-pupil values were taken as provided, using state-reported enrollment (WP §3.4). Readers cannot tell which denominator produced Table 3.
- [checkable] Other steps are unspecified in the article:
  - which Mapping Inequality release was used (only a 2020 retrieval date is given, p.27) and how overlapping or null-grade polygons were handled;
  - the map projection used for square-mile areas;
  - how exact cutpoint values (1.5, 2.5, 3.5) are assigned (p.10);
  - which schools on polygon edges or in overlapping polygons are kept (p.10);
  - which CBSA delineation vintage was used, and how districts spanning more than one CBSA are assigned;
  - the inflation deflator ("adjusted for inflation and denominated in 2018 USD," p.7);
  - the names of the F-33 revenue variables and the enrollment variable;
  - which SEDA 4.0 file and weight variable were used;
  - whether the time-series panels are balanced, and which years they contain. Table 1 says "1989–2018" (p.9), but the figures show four points roughly ten years apart (p.13, p.17).
- [checkable] Some statements about the specification conflict or leave gaps. The Methods section says "All outcomes are weighted for district or school enrollment" (p.10), but Table 5 is weighted by the number of tests (p.19). Figure 3's caption says "A to D indicators" and Figure 4's says "A to C indicators" (p.13, p.17). Neither caption says whether CBSA FE are included or whether the plotted values are raw or model-adjusted means. The captions mention cluster-robust SEs, but neither figure shows intervals. The reported F statistic and R² are never defined (e.g., the joint test of A/B/C? within or overall R²?).
- [judgment] Mapping Inequality's third-version (2023) release added more than 100 maps. A replicator who downloads the polygons today will therefore start from a different HOLC universe than the October 2020 extract used here, and I did not find an archived copy of the 2020 extract. NERD\$ is not currently self-serve: the Edunomics page says the module is being updated and asks users to email the lab. SEDA 4.0 school pooled CS files are still downloadable from edopportunity.org. Markley's tabulations are on OSF.
- [judgment] Because all inputs are public, restricted data give no reason to withhold code. For a 2026 article, "no statement, no package" is below journal-era norms, and the unavailable supplement holds every robustness check and every time-series coefficient.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Trust the cross-sectional tables (Tables 2–5) more than the time-series claims. The tables fully report estimates and uncertainty. Do not rely on Figure 3 at all. For how district finance gaps changed over time, use Supplemental Table A4(A), or the dollar-denominated Figure 4/Table 4 in the 2021 EdWorkingPaper (ai21-363), bearing in mind that it is an earlier sample and specification. The claim that district finance gaps are "persistent and growing over time" (p.20) cannot be checked from the published article.
- Before citing the Figure 4 trend numbers (13.4 pp, about 35 pp, beyond −0.08; p.17–18), check them against Supplemental Table A4(B). They do not match the plotted series.
- Use −0.225 SD as the Northeast D-school average score (Table 5, p.19), not the −0.023 quoted in the text. Treat the Midwest school-spending gaps as statistically insignificant, as Table 3 shows.
- If you try to replicate, ask the authors for these items first:
  - the exact HOLC polygon file (2020 vintage);
  - the district crosswalk, including the NYC sub-district and charter point assignments;
  - the CBSA crosswalk;
  - the deflator series;
  - the F-33 and NERD\$ variable lists and the enrollment denominators;
  - the SEDA file and weight names;
  - an explanation of the 5,124 vs. 6,890 school count.
- A good first test is to recompute the district weighted average and grade from the p.10 formula and check the grade counts against Supplemental Table A1. If your counts are far off, the gap is probably from a different HOLC version, NYC, or charter handling rather than from the regressions.
- Treat the Simpson's-index trend (Figure 4C) with caution until you confirm how race categories were harmonized. NCES race categories changed during the 2008–09 to 2018–19 decade, which is exactly when the index rises most, and the paper does not say how it handled the change.
- The reported "Constant = D mean" values (e.g., \$14,402, p.12) depend on how the software normalizes fixed effects. Expect small differences in the constants, but not in the A/B/C contrasts, when you re-run with a different estimator.

**Detailed Commentary:**

What the paper states, taken at face value, is more than many descriptive papers give. The estimand is a within-CBSA difference in means by HOLC grade, with D as the reference. The paper gives an explicit area-weighting formula, explicit discretization bins, stated weights, CBSA clustering, and full regression output with Ns. A replicator with the same inputs could write the regression code from p.10 and the table notes alone. The problem sits upstream of the regressions, in building the analytic dataset. Nearly every consequential choice in the HOLC-to-district and HOLC-to-school linkage is either unstated in the published article or was documented only in the 2021 working paper and then dropped: NYC's 32 geographic districts, point-assigned charter LEAs, "E" polygons, the OLS-vs-EB choice, and the seven-category diversity index. The NYC substitution alone could move a meaningful share of the 608 Northeast districts in Table 2 (p.12). Without it, a replicator using the cited TIGER/Line file would treat New York City as one district. Also, the TIGER reference URL (p.28) points to the Census cartographic-boundary page, not the TIGER/Line school-district files.

The most consequential problem is an exhibit error, not a documentation gap. Figure 3 is presented as district per-pupil revenue from 1989 to 2018 in 2018 dollars. On the rendered page, its panels A, B, and D are the diversity series from Figure 4 under revenue titles. The panel C "state revenue" series (0.40–0.80) matches nothing in the article either. The text around Figure 3 (p.13–14) and the conclusion that district finance gaps are "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018" (p.20) therefore have no valid supporting exhibit in the article. The only numeric support is Supplemental Table A4(A), which was not available to this review. The 2021 working paper had a correct dollar-scale version, so this looks like a production error rather than a missing analysis. Still, the published record as it stands cannot support that claim.

Some numbers in the article disagree with each other. Table 1's 5,124 performance-sample schools against Table 5's Ns of 6,890, 5,193, and 6,183 is the clearest case. It matters because Table 1 is the reader's only guide to how the samples were built. The Northeast score in the text (−0.023) versus the table (−0.225), and the Midwest spending gaps described as significant when the table shows no stars, are smaller problems. But they suggest the text was not re-checked against the final tables. The Figure 4 text values also do not match the plotted series, and some of them appear word-for-word in the 2021 working paper. That suggests they may have been carried over from an earlier panel rather than recomputed. The working paper itself gives two different sizes for the diversity panel: 4,677 schools in 590 districts in its §4.1, and 4,693 schools in 478 districts in 31 CBSAs in its fn. 22. The published Table 1 gives 4,677 schools, 590 districts, and 118 CBSAs (p.9). The panel's construction is therefore not pinned down anywhere.

On access, I checked the sources directly. SEDA 4.0 school-level pooled CS files are still publicly downloadable. The cited purl (db586ns4974) now redirects to a "SEDA has moved" page, and the 4.0-specific purl is vb140hd2862. Mapping Inequality is downloadable, but it is now on its third version (2023), which added more than 100 maps, so the October 2020 extract the authors used is not the current download. NERD\$ requires contacting Edunomics Lab while its module is being rebuilt. Markley's tabulations are on OSF (the reference's DOI resolves to the OSF preprint). F-33 and CCD data are available through ELSi. So the inputs can be recovered with effort, but there is version drift on the HOLC side and a gatekeeping step for NERD\$.

On the rating: I rate this Weak, near the Adequate boundary. If the question were only whether the cross-sectional Tables 2–5 can be understood and approximately regenerated, Adequate would be fair. The paper does not get there because it has no data or code statement and no package despite fully public inputs, it omits sample-defining steps it previously documented, its sample counts do not reconcile, and its finance time-series exhibit is the wrong figure. Together these mean that part of the paper's claim structure (the longitudinal finance and diversity trends) cannot be verified from the article, and the rest can be approximated but not exactly reproduced. My confidence is limited mainly because the supplement (Tables A1–A8, Figures A1–A12) was unavailable. It may resolve the Table 1/Table 5 count gap and the Figure 4 text values, though it cannot fix the published Figure 3.
